passages.t: Dogs prowling at night, and ‘I will sing of Your strength in the morning’
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “A Miktam of David, when Saul sent men to watch David’s house in order to kill him” (verse 1). The prayer begins, “Deliver me from my enemies, O my God; protect me from those who rise against me” (verse 1).

He says the attack has no cause. “Fierce men conspire against me for no transgression or sin of my own, O LORD” (verse 3).

Twice the enemies are pictured the same way. “They return in the evening, snarling like dogs and prowling around the city” (verses 6 and 14). They think no one is listening: “For who can hear us?” (verse 7). “But You, O LORD, laugh at them” (verse 8).

Twice, too, comes a refrain of trust: God is “my strength” and “my fortress” (verses 9 and 17). The night ends in song. “But I will sing of Your strength and proclaim Your loving devotion in the morning” (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
The story is in 1 Samuel 19. “Then Saul sent messengers to David’s house to watch him and kill him in the morning” (1 Samuel 19:11). David's wife Michal, Saul's own daughter, warned him and let him down through a window. The psalm's night of watching and morning of song fits that night well. The book page explains the headings.

Dogs in the ancient world were rarely pets. Packs of half-wild dogs roamed towns at night, eating scraps and growling over food. Calling enemies ‘dogs’ was a strong insult.

The psalm also speaks of ‘all the nations’ (verses 5 and 8), which sounds more like a king facing foreign enemies. Some scholars think it was written later for a king and linked to David's story by its heading. Others think David, already anointed as the next king, saw his danger in larger terms.
passages.later: Paul knew nights like this. In Damascus his enemies watched the city gates day and night to kill him, and he too was let down through a window in the wall, in a basket (Acts 9:24-25; 2 Corinthians 11:33).
passages.hard: Verse 11 asks God, “Do not kill them”, and verse 13 says, “consume them till they are no more” (verse 13). Is that a contradiction? One common reading is that David asks for a slow, visible judgment, so that people will not forget it, and that ‘consume’ means ending their power. Others think the prayer simply holds a real tension, as prayers in danger often do. Both readings agree on the goal: “so it may be known to the ends of the earth that God rules over Jacob” (verse 13).
passages.asks:
Night in this psalm is the time of danger. Morning is the time of rescue and song. Many people know what it is to lie awake while fears prowl like dogs.

The psalm does not tell you the dogs will vanish. It tells you to watch for God (verse 9), and it promises that morning will come. Say verse 16 to yourself at night, and see if it is true at dawn.
